assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opening a genuinely new observational window: a cubic-kilometre Antarctic ice detector that measured a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos, followed by evidence for individual sources (the blazar TXS 0506+056 in 2017-18 and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 in 2022) and a Galactic-plane signal. This is exactly the kind of instrument-driven discovery I respect: decades of calibration, ice characterisation and systematics control before anyone believed the signal.
assessment.attribution: The detector concept and decades-long leadership are most clearly associated with Halzen; Karle and Spiering are credited for detector construction, analysis and the collaboration's growth. IceCube is a large collaboration, so any three names under-represent the work. I am relying on my general knowledge of the roles rather than verifying them here.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is confirmed through several independent analysis channels, and KM3NeT's and Baikal-GVD's results are broadly consistent. The source associations are at a lower significance than the diffuse flux, but the discovery claim does not depend on them. Timing is good.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to credit the 2017-18 source identification, the diffuse-flux discovery, or the detector concept, since each points to different people
Collaboration of several hundred; the three-person limit is difficult
Statistical strength of individual source associations is still modest

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock is a clean, original invention (the magic-wavelength idea) that took timekeeping to the 1e-18 level and now enables tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. Impact is broad and lasting and the physics is easy to explain with comparisons of scale.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept; Ye led the realisation to the highest accuracy and stability, including the strontium clock and frequency-comb connections. Two laureates fit well. Others (for example ion-clock groups) are outside this candidate's credit but could raise a boundary question.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) have reproduced and compared the clocks. Recognition is mature and not premature.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier Nobel recognition of frequency combs and ion trapping may make the committee view it as a continuation
Credit relative to ion-clock and Hall/Hansch-related work needs care
Outside my own field of astroparticle physics, so I would defer to atomic-physics colleagues on fine attribution

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ground-based imaging atmospheric Cherenkov astronomy created a new window on non-thermal processes in the Universe, with several hundred TeV sources and a connection to cosmic-ray origin. H.E.S.S. in particular delivered the first resolved TeV images of supernova remnants and the Galactic-plane survey. This is a detector-plus-technique achievement very close to my own field.
assessment.attribution: Hofmann led H.E.S.S. and Aharonian provided the theory and the scientific programme. The credit is a fair two-person configuration, but it omits the Whipple, HEGRA and MAGIC pioneers (Weekes, for the first TeV detection of the Crab and the imaging technique), and I am aware that the allocation is contentious.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and independently confirmed by H.E.S.S., MAGIC, VERITAS and now LHAASO. The community consensus on the existence and breadth of the TeV sky is solid.
uncertainties: Technique pioneers such as the Whipple group may be more decisive than the credited names
Whether the field is best seen as a continuous programme without one decisive discovery
Allocation between instrument builders and scientists

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum-enhanced interferometry started from Caves' 1981 proposal to reduce quantum noise with squeezed vacuum and reached practical use in the LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 detectors. It is an important and visible quantum-metrology advance, and it directly improves the sensitivity of the instruments that detected gravitational waves.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the decisive theoretical idea. Schnabel and others realised the large-scale squeezed-light source in GEO600; Mavalvala led the LIGO implementation and its extension to frequency-dependent squeezing. Kimble's squeezing demonstrations and the Bell Labs experiments by Slusher and colleagues are also important, so this three-name set is not unique.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is routinely used in operating detectors (GEO600 since 2010, LIGO since 2019) and is independently demonstrated, so maturity is good. Impact on detection rate is documented.
uncertainties: Competing credit for first demonstrations (Slusher, Kimble) and for theory
The prize value is an enabling improvement to a detector already recognised in 2017
Possible overlap with candidate B004, which concerns the continuous-variable aspect

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson by ATLAS and CMS completed the Standard Model and was one of the great instrument achievements of particle physics. The detectors, triggers and calibration needed for it are a story I appreciate as a detector builder. The theory was recognised in 2013, but the experimental discovery is a separate and lasting achievement.
assessment.attribution: Credit is hard: thousands of people built the experiments. The credited names include spokespersons and concept leaders; I choose Gianotti (ATLAS spokesperson at the time of the discovery), Della Negra (CMS concept and early leadership) and Virdee (CMS leadership and calorimetry), but Jenni (ATLAS founder-spokesperson) is an equally defensible choice. The Nobel statutes make a collaboration prize difficult.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by two independent experiments with later measurements of couplings and spin-parity; the interpretation is stable and mature.
uncertainties: Statutes limit to three people and an institution-level award is not allowed, so the allocation could be seen as arbitrary
Whether the prize would be perceived as redundant after 2013
Leadership credit versus decisive scientific contribution

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first horizon-scale images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022) are a landmark in observational astrophysics, enabled by global VLBI at 1.3 mm. The result makes a direct test of strong-field gravity and black-hole shadows. The 2020 prize recognised black-hole theory and the Galactic Centre orbits, so the imaging is a complementary experimental achievement.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept in 2000; Doeleman led the EHT technical and collaboration programme; Zensus was a leading VLBI institution builder. The collaboration comprises over 200 members and credit is spread across algorithms, correlators, telescope arrays and calibration.
assessment.maturity: Two independent source images and multi-epoch M87* data (2017, 2018) are consistent, and polarisation imaging has been added. Interpretation of the ring is stable, but image reconstruction dependence and the astrophysical modelling still evolve.
uncertainties: Reconstruction systematics and model-dependence of image interpretation
Large collaboration, and diffuse credit for algorithms (e.g. imaging methods)
The extent to which this tests general relativity at a precision beyond the 2017 LIGO results

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators are a conceptual advance that created a major class of materials and was experimentally realised in HgTe quantum wells. Impact on condensed-matter physics and on spintronics and topological ideas is large and durable. This lies outside my own expertise, so I would rely on colleagues for the finer assessment.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction and defined the Z2 classification. Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation (with Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes proposing HgTe, who are not in the credited names). Using this candidate rather than B038 avoids mixing in the quantum anomalous Hall effect, which has separate credit.
assessment.maturity: Observed in multiple materials and by several groups, with 3D topological insulators also established. Maturity is good, though some transport quantisation results are debated.
uncertainties: Predicting versus observing credit; Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the Xue group are missing from this set
Overlap with Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz topological recognition in 2016
Limited expertise in this field on my part

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar timing arrays gave the first evidence (2023) for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background, which opens a new frequency band and is likely from supermassive black-hole binaries. It is built on exquisitely careful timing of millisecond pulsars, which I respect as a measurement achievement.
assessment.attribution: Credit is distributed among the NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, InPTA and CPTA collaborations. Hobbs, Kramer and Siemens represent different arrays, but the field's founding ideas (Hellings-Downs, Detweiler, Foster-Backer) are not in this set. Allocation is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Premature: the 2023 evidence is roughly 3 to 4 sigma with the Hellings-Downs correlation, and has not yet reached discovery-level significance. Source identification and spectral interpretation are open.
uncertainties: Not yet a firm detection and origin unresolved
Large multi-collaboration credit problem
Better to wait for IPTA combined data
